questions.knowledge_point: Determining Vertical Asymptotes of Rational Functions by Factoring the Numerator and Denominator
questions.worked_solution:
We start by factoring the function as much as possible and canceling the common factors:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}-4}{2{x}^{2}+5x+2} & =\frac{{x}^{2}-{2}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}+4x+x+2} \\  & =\frac{(x+2)(x-2)}{2x(x+2)+(x+2)} \\  & =\frac{(x+2)(x-2)}{(2x+1)(x+2)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(x+2)}(x-2)}{(2x+1)\cancel{(x+2)}} \\  & =\frac{x-2}{2x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now set the denominator equal to zero:

$$
2x+1=0\,⟹\,x=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the *only* vertical asymptote is at $x=-\frac{1}{2}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying When a Rational Function has no Vertical Asymptotes
questions.worked_solution:
Let's simplify the expression by factoring both the numerator and the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}}{2x+4} & =\frac{{x}^{2}(x+2)}{2(x+2)}=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the denominator is never zero, we conclude that this function has no vertical asymptotes. A plot of the function is below. Note that it is not defined at $x=-2.$

questions.worked_solution:
Let's simplify the expression by factoring both the numerator and the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x+2)({x}^{4}+{x}^{3}-6{x}^{2})}{{x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}} & =\frac{{x}^{2}(x+2)({x}^{2}+x-6)}{{x}^{2}(x+2)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{{x}^{2}(x+2)}({x}^{2}+x-6)}{\cancel{{x}^{2}(x+2)}} \\  & ={x}^{2}+x-6\end{aligned}
$$

Since the denominator is never zero, we conclude that this function has no vertical asymptotes. A plot of the function is below. Note that it is not defined at $x=-2$ and $x=0.$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Vertical Asymptotes for the Sum of Two Rational Functions
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's put the two terms over a common denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{2x}+\frac{3}{4x} & =\frac{5(2)+3}{4x}=\frac{13}{4x}\end{aligned}
$$

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we proceed to set the denominator equal to zero and get

$$
4x=0\,⟹\,x=0.
$$

Therefore, the vertical asymptotes are at $x=0.$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining Vertical Asymptotes of Rational Functions by Factoring the Numerator and Denominator
questions.worked_solution:
We start by factoring the function as much as possible and canceling the common factors:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{8x-16}{{x}^{2}-6x+8} & =\frac{8(x-2)}{(x-2)(x-4)} \\  & =\frac{8\cancel{(x-2)}}{\cancel{(x-2)}(x-4)} \\  & =\frac{8}{x-4}\end{aligned}
$$

We now set the denominator equal to zero:

$$
x-4=0\,⟹\,x=4
$$

So the *only* vertical asymptote is at $x=4.$
